html:
Between 1937 and 1939, purges in communist Mongolia killed tens of thousands of people, a large share of them Buddhist lamas, and destroyed almost all of the country's monasteries. Mongolians call it the Great Repression.

Before this, the Buddhist church was the richest and strongest institution in the land, and a large part of all men were monks. The communist government saw it as a rival. Under the leader Khorloogiin Choibalsan, with advisers from the Soviet NKVD, the campaign followed the Great Purge then under way in Stalin's Soviet Union. Lamas were shot or sent to labour camps; younger monks were forced back to lay life.

Hundreds of monasteries were burned or pulled down, with their libraries and art. A few survived as museums, among them Erdene Zuu, and Gandan in Ulaanbaatar reopened in 1944 under tight control. Buddhism revived openly only after the democratic revolution of 1990.
